To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The initial levels of flexibility or vertical jump ability of elite gymnasts did not affect straight leg raise range-of-motion (ROM) or counter movement jump performance following different volumes (15 s or 30 s) of stretching or potentiating exercises (3 or 5 sets of 5 jumps).
the initial levels and flexibility and vertical jump abilities of elite gymnasts have no effect on the response to warm up protocols with different volumes of stretching or potentiating exercises.

The initial levels of flexibility (straight leg raise range of motions) and vertical jump ability (counter movement jump) of elite gymnastics athletes have no effect on their responses to warm up protocols that differ in stretching and potenating exercise volumes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the physical fitness of elite athletes and their performance following different warm-up protocols.
the effects of different volumes of stretching on the range of motion and vertical jump ability of elite gymnasts.
the effect of the volume of stretching and poteniating exercises on the performance of elite gymnasts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the initial levels (baseline) of flexibility and vertical jumping ability have no effect upon the response of elite gymnasts when they perform different volumes of stretching exercises and potentiating (jumping) exercises.

a warm up protocol consisting of long (30 s) stretching of the main leg muscles followed by 3 sets of potentiating exercises (5 tuck jumps) would be the optimal warm up protocol for improving performance and preventing injury.

the initial levels (baseline) of flexibility and vertical jumping ability have no effect in the response of elite gymnasts when performing different warm up protocols that differ in the volumes of stretching and jumping exercises, and that stretching of the main leg muscles for only 15s has no effect on range of motion of elite gymnasts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the initial levels and the subsequent responses of flexibility and vertical jumping ability are independent of the initial levels of each of the two parameters.
30 s stretching and 3 sets of potentiating exercises are necessary for elite athletes to achieve a significant increase in both flexibility and jump performance during warm up.

the initial levels for flexibility and vertical jump performance have no effect on the response to stretching and potentiatiing exercises, and that 3 sets of potentiating exercise (3x5 tucks) during the warm up protocol are necessary to increase CMJ in these highly trained elite gymnasts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the initial levels (or baseline) levels of flexibility and jump ability of elite gymnasts do not alter the response of these gymnasts to warm-up protocols differing in stretching exercise volumes.

the volume of stretching and poteniating exercises should be carefully planned for each athlete, as the effects on flexibility and CMJ differ between the athletes, depending on their initial levels of flexibility.
3 sets of potentiating exercises (tuck jumps in our case) should be included in the warm up of elite gymnasts.
